text: Of things some are in our power, and others are not.
And the things in our power are by nature free, not subject to restraint nor hindrance
If you love an earthen vessel, say it is an earthen vessel which you love; for when it has been broken, you will not be disturbed.
note: The chapter goes on to say the same of a wife or child. A hard saying: never press it on someone newly bereaved.

text: Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things
When then we are impeded or disturbed or grieved, let us never blame others, but ourselves, that is, our opinions.
Seek not that the things which happen should happen as you wish; but wish the things which happen to be as they are, and you will have a tranquil flow of life.
Disease is an impediment to the body, but not to the will, unless the will itself chooses. Lameness is an impediment to the leg, but not to the will.
On the occasion of every accident (event) that befals you, remember to turn to yourself and inquire what power you have for turning it to use.
Never say about any thing, I have lost it, but say I have restored it.
note: The chapter continues with a dead child and a dead wife. Say it gently, if at all, to someone in fresh grief.

text: So long as he may allow you, take care of it as a thing which belongs to another, as travellers do with their inn.
If you would have your children and your wife and your friends to live for ever, you are silly; for you would have the things which are not in your power to be in your power

Remember that in life you ought to behave as at a banquet. Suppose that something is carried round and is opposite to you. Stretch out your hand and take a portion with decency. Suppose that it passes by you. Do not detain it.
For this is your duty, to act well the part that is given to you; but to select the part, belongs to another.
You can be invincible, if you enter into no contest in which it is not in your power to conquer.
Remember that it is not he who reviles you or strikes you, who insults you, but it is your opinion about these things as being insulting.
For if you once gain time and delay, you will more easily master yourself.

Let death and exile and every other thing which appears dreadful be daily before your eyes; but most of all death: and you will never think of any thing mean nor will you desire any thing extravagantly.
And let silence be the general rule, or let only what is necessary be said, and in few words.
Every thing has two handles, the one by which it may be borne, the other by which it may not.
These reasonings do not cohere: I am richer than you, therefore I am better than you; I am more eloquent than you, therefore I am better than you.
For even sheep do not vomit up their grass and show to the shepherds how much they have eaten
The condition and characteristic of a philosopher is this: he expects all advantage and all harm from himself.
How long will you then still defer thinking yourself worthy of the best things, and in no matter transgressing the distinctive reason?
note: Chapter 51 in most modern editions; Long's translation has 52 chapters.

text: Lead me, O Zeus, and thou O Destiny, The way that I am bid by you to go: To follow I am ready.
note: Epictetus is quoting Cleanthes. Chapter 53 in most modern editions.

text: Anytus and Melitus are able indeed to kill me, but they cannot harm me.
note: Epictetus is quoting Socrates from Plato's Apology. Chapter 53 in most modern editions.

text: I must die. Must I then die lamenting? I must be put in chains. Must I then also lament?
We must make the best use that we can of the things which are in our power, and use the rest according to their nature.
For what else can I do, a lame old man, than sing hymns to God?
It is circumstances (difficulties) which show what men are.
Every habit and faculty is maintained and increased by the corresponding actions: the habit of walking by walking, the habit of running by running.
The philosopher's school, ye men, is a surgery: you ought not to go out of it with pleasure, but with pain.
He is free who lives as he wishes to live; who is neither subject to compulsion nor to hindrance, nor to force
